name: Calf raise
angleNote: Plantarflexion: 0° = foot at right angles to the shin, negative = heel below the step (stretch), 40° = up on the toes. Knee at the origin.

segments.note: Knee→ankle, and ankle→ball of the foot (the point the floor pushes on), in metres. Closed chain: the floor carries the foot's own weight, so no limb weight is added.

strengthCurve.label: Plantarflexor strength
strengthCurve.note: Relative plantarflexion torque, assumed strongest with the calf stretched and weakest high on the toes. Approximate shape.
strengthCurve.source: TODO: verify against published torque–angle data

muscles.name: Gastrocnemius
muscles.note: Crosses the knee too: with the knee bent (seated) it is slack and contributes much less.

muscles.name: Soleus
muscles.note: Crosses the ankle only, so it works whatever the knee angle.

phases.name: Stretch
phases.text: Heel below the step. The ball of the foot is furthest in front of the ankle, so the moment arm is at its largest.

phases.name: Mid-range
phases.text: Moment arm = foot lever × cos(angle): it shrinks slowly as you rise.

phases.name: Top
phases.text: High on the toes: smaller moment arm, but the calves are weakest here too.

variants.name: Single-leg standing calf raise (dumbbell)
variants.notes: Closed chain: the floor pushes up on the ball of the foot with your whole body weight plus the dumbbell. Torque = (body + m)·g·foot lever·cos(angle).

variants.name: Standing calf raise machine (two legs)
variants.notes: Each leg carries half your body weight plus half the load (the load slider is per leg).

variants.name: Seated calf raise machine
variants.notes: The load sits on the knees, so body weight isn't lifted. With the knee bent the gastrocnemius is slack; the 0.5 factor on it is an estimate, not a measured value.
